And , like S&amp;P Global , the Fitch Ratings report anticipates more closures and mergers . 
@@118966434 <h> The Humanities and the Power of Emotions and Ideas <p> In his essay " A Defence of Poetry " ( 1821 ) , English Romantic poet Percy Bysshe Shelley describes poets as " the unacknowledged legislators of the world . " Shelley argues that poets , though seldom recognized or rewarded for their influence , play a vital role in shaping society 's moral , cultural and intellectual frameworks . <p> He believes that poets -- and , by extension , other creative thinkers -- profoundly shape how people perceive the world , influencing values , emotions and ideas in ways that formal laws or governments can not . <p> Shelley 's assertion rests on the belief that poetry and the arts can tap into universal truths , challenge established norms and inspire social and moral progress . In this sense , poets are legislators of thought and feeling , even if their contributions often go unnoticed by the public . <h> Most Popular <p> In contrast , economist John Maynard Keynes remarked that " if you scratch a businessman , you will find a second-rate economist . " Most businesspeople , Keynes thought , rely on oversimplified or outdated economic principles , adopted uncritically . He suggests that while these individuals believe they are acting with rationality and expertise , their understanding of economics tends to be shallow , built on flawed or second-rate ideas . <p> Keynes 's point is that economic theory is complex and effective decision-making requires a deeper understanding than what is typically practiced in the business world . He also warned that economic theories , even when flawed , have significant real-world consequences , as those in business often unknowingly adhere to outdated ideas , often with detrimental effects . <p> Both Shelley and Keynes emphasize how intellectual contributions -- whether from poets or economists -- can shape society in profound but unacknowledged ways . Whether it is the unseen influence of artists or the unexamined adherence to economic principles , their insights underscore how ideas shape the world , even if those implementing them fail to fully grasp their origins or significance . <p> In a world preoccupied with material power -- military , economic or political -- it is easy to overlook the invisible forces that truly shape human history . Yet the most enduring and transformative powers lie not in weapons or wealth , but in the realm of ideas , emotions and values . These forces drive revolutions , inspire social movements and define civilizations . To study the humanities is to engage with these deep , often unseen drivers of human behavior . <p> The humanities focus on the intangible yet powerful forces that shape human consciousness . They reveal that the mind is the most potent engine of transformation . Ideas born from intellectual inquiry and the emotions that guide human action profoundly influence how societies evolve , adapt and sometimes collapse . Armies may win battles , but it is the ideas behind them -- nationalism , justice , freedom or tyranny -- that win wars . Economies may generate wealth , but it is the values and emotions of hope , fear , ambition or greed that shape economic decisions and social structures . <p> History is a testament to the power of ideas and emotions . Ideologies like democracy , communism and capitalism have reshaped continents . Emotions such as fear , pride and hope have sparked revolutions and toppled regimes . By studying these invisible forces , the humanities illuminate the true drivers of history -- forces far more enduring than any empire or economy . They help us navigate these currents , offering insights into the ideologies , values and emotions that shape human behavior and helping us better understand both progress and conflict . <p> The most profound changes in history come not from wealth accumulation or territorial conquest , but from shifts in how people think , feel and perceive the world . From Enlightenment ideals that fueled revolutions to civil rights movements powered by the emotions of justice and equality , history is shaped by the mind 's capacity to envision a different world . <p> The mind , not the sword , is the ultimate source of power , and the humanities unlock its potential . By engaging with ideologies , values and emotions , the humanities help us understand the essence of human life -- what we strive for , fear and value -- and how these forces propel or restrain us . <p> Power is often associated with political , military or economic dominance -- what we typically think of as hard power . When considering soft power , we often think of mass media , cultural exports like films and music , or charismatic leaders . However , an equally potent and often overlooked form of power is the power of ideas and ideologies . This influence shapes how societies understand themselves , how individuals interpret the world and how both envision their future . <h> Editors ' Picks <p> Ideas -- whether political , philosophical or cultural -- are the lenses through which we see the world . They shape our assumptions , values and aspirations . Concepts like democracy , freedom , equality and justice are not abstract ideals ; they are frameworks that guide real-world governance , law and society . These ideas determine how we define fairness , what rights we prioritize and how we structure institutions . They influence decisions at both individual and national levels , shaping everything from voting and protesting to policymaking on a global scale . <p> Take ideologies like capitalism , socialism , liberalism or conservatism . These belief systems have driven historical change and continue to influence debates about how societies should function . A capitalist society prizes market competition and individual wealth , while socialism values collective ownership and economic equality . These systems are not merely material ; they are rooted in fundamental beliefs about human nature and fairness . Ideas such as these guide economic policies , elections and social movements . Whether or not we realize it , the ideologies we adopt shape the structure of our lives . <p> Ideas also shape how we interpret events . A revolution might be seen as a righteous struggle for freedom or a dangerous upheaval , depending on the observer 's ideological lens . Climate change can be framed as an urgent crisis or as an overstated threat , depending on underlying values . Ideologies provide narratives that help make sense of complex issues and suggest what actions should be taken . This interpretive power not only shapes policy but also molds public opinion and personal decisions . <p> The power of ideas is especially evident in how societies construct their values . Take the concept of human rights , which gained prominence in the 20th century . The belief that all individuals deserve certain inalienable rights has reshaped global legal systems , international relations and civil rights movements . Human rights are not enforced by any one country or institution , yet the idea has become so ingrained that it now governs global norms . It is not military or economic power that spread this ideology -- it is the power of an idea . <p> Revolutions and social movements offer some of the clearest examples of the transformative force of ideas . The American Revolution , the French Revolution and the civil rights movements were driven not by military might or economic sanctions , but by new ideas about liberty , equality , citizenship and justice . These movements were powered by shifts in consciousness -- a collective realization that existing systems were unjust and that alternatives were possible . The ideas behind these movements redefined what people believed they deserved and what kind of society they wanted to build . <p> Even in daily life , the influence of ideas is clear . Gender roles , race and identity are shaped by the prevailing ideologies of the time . Feminism challenged long-held beliefs about gender equality , reshaping opportunities and rights for future generations . Similarly , movements like Black Lives Matter have forced society to confront systemic racism and rethink justice . These movements show that ideas have the power to redefine societal norms and foster transformative change . <p> Today , ideologies continue to shape society , particularly through education , media and intellectual discourse . Universities are not just places where technical skills are taught ; they are battlegrounds where ideas are debated , formed and disseminated . From classrooms to newsrooms , ideas are constantly being challenged and spread , influencing how society thinks about issues like climate change , inequality , immigration and health care . The intellectual frameworks built in these environments eventually trickle down into broader public consciousness . <p> To underestimate the power of ideas is to ignore one of the most potent forces in human history . Military power can win battles and economic power can build empires , but it is the power of ideas that ultimately shapes civilizations . Ideas guide how we interpret the world , what we value and what we strive for . They are the invisible architects of our collective future , shaping the world we live in and the one we hope to create . By recognizing the power of ideas , we gain a better understanding of the forces that drive change -- politically , economically and philosophically . <p> The humanities are the disciplines that focus on meaning , perception and values , examining the deeper , often intangible aspects of human existence . Unlike the natural sciences , which explore the nature of the physical world , or the social sciences , which analyze behavior in theoretical and scientific terms , the humanities address the internal landscapes of individuals and societies -- our hopes , fears , dreams , illusions , emotions and sometimes our nightmares . <p> At the heart of the humanities lies the study of ideas and ideologies . Disciplines like literature , philosophy , history , art and religious studies explore how ideas form , spread and evolve over time , shaping identities , cultures and societies . History is not just a record of events but a way to understand the driving ideas behind movements such as freedom , justice or progress . Philosophy challenges us to interrogate these concepts , asking fundamental questions about existence , ethics and knowledge . Literature expresses the emotional and psychological dimensions of human experience , revealing hidden desires and fears . <p> Humans are meaning makers , constantly interpreting the world through various lenses . The humanities provide tools to examine and question the narratives that shape our understanding . A literary analysis of a novel reveals not just the plot but also the underlying themes and symbols that speak to broader social or psychological truths . Similarly , the study of art reveals how visual representations convey ideologies , evoke emotions or challenge cultural norms . The humanities probe the nature of myths , symbols and metaphors , helping us make sense of life 's complexities . <p> Perception is another key focus of the humanities . How do we interpret the world ? How do culture , language and history shape our perceptions of reality ? The humanities tackle these questions . Art history , for instance , studies how different cultures perceive beauty , form and meaning through visual expression . Linguistics explores how language shapes thought and interaction , while cultural studies examine how media , pop culture and mass communication frame our perceptions of identity , gender , race and class . Through this lens , the humanities reveal that our experiences are always mediated by cultural context . <p> Values are also central to the humanities . They are not just personal preferences but foundational beliefs that shape moral , ethical and political decisions . The humanities challenge us to consider questions like : What is justice ? What constitutes a good life ? What are our responsibilities to others ? By studying the moral philosophies of thinkers like Aristotle , Kant or Confucius or analyzing ethical dilemmas in literature or history , we learn how values are constructed , debated and enacted . In doing so , the humanities cultivate critical thinking about our place in the world and our obligations to others . <p> One of the most profound contributions of the humanities is their exploration of human emotions . Literature , art , music and drama have long been vehicles for expressing and examining the full range of human emotions -- from love , joy and hope to fear , anger and despair . Emotions , while personal , are shaped by cultural narratives and shared experiences . The humanities allow us to see both the universal aspects of human emotions and the particular ways they are experienced in different historical and cultural contexts . <p> The humanities also provide insight into human fantasies and dreams -- how people envision alternative realities or futures . Through literature , film and art , the humanities explore how societies understand their current realities and imagine different possibilities . Utopian and dystopian literature reflects societal hopes and fears about political , technological or environmental futures . Myths and folklore reveal how cultures use stories to explain the unknown , often expressing collective desires or anxieties . <p> Nightmares , both personal and societal , are equally a focus of the humanities . Whether it 's the existential dread explored in Kafka 's novels or the cultural traumas examined in postcolonial literature , the humanities confront the uglier sides of human experience . They grapple with suffering , oppression , alienation and fear , revealing how these forces shape individual lives and collective histories . The humanities do not merely document atrocities like war , genocide and social injustice ; they explore the ethical and emotional dimensions of human suffering , compelling us to confront uncomfortable truths about ourselves and the world . <p> The diminishing presence of the humanities in contemporary education risks leaving individuals and societies without a deeper understanding of these fundamental aspects of human life . When education is reduced to purely technical or utilitarian goals -- focusing solely on preparing students for the job market -- the broader mission of cultivating reflective , morally engaged citizens is neglected . The humanities foster empathy , critical thinking and the ability to question assumptions , all of which are essential not only for personal growth but for the health of democratic societies . <p> The humanities are essential because they study the ideas , values , perceptions and emotions that shape human existence . They encourage us to reflect on the meaning of life , challenge dominant ideologies and explore the full range of human emotions and desires . By engaging with the humanities , we learn not just about the world , but about ourselves and how we make sense of life 's complexities . In doing so , we deepen our understanding of what it means to be human . <p> The history of emotions is one of the most dynamic fields within the humanities , illustrating that emotions are not simply universal , biological experiences , but are deeply shaped by cultural , social and historical contexts . This emerging field reveals that emotions are influenced by norms , values and institutions and in turn , play an active role in shaping history . <p> Among the key issues that the history of emotions studies are these : <p> Emotions as historically and culturally contingent : Emotions are not static across time or place . What is considered an appropriate or expected emotional response in one culture or era may be seen as inappropriate or strange in another . For instance , the modern concept of romantic love was largely absent in premodern societies , where marriage was more often determined by social , political or economic factors than by personal affection . <p> Emotional standards and regulation : Throughout history , societies have established norms for emotional expression . In medieval Europe , emotions such as grief or joy were expected to be expressed differently depending on one 's social status , gender or role . The Stoics in ancient Greece advocated for emotional restraint , while certain religious traditions encouraged open displays of devotion , guilt or fear of divine judgment . <p> The role of emotions in power and politics : Emotions are deeply intertwined with power structures . Historical elites have frequently used emotional manipulation to maintain control . Monarchs and religious authorities in early modern Europe promoted fear of divine punishment to uphold social order , while the French Revolution saw emotional expressions of patriotism and outrage as crucial for mobilizing the masses . <p> The concept of emotional communities : Historian Barbara Rosenwein introduced the idea of emotional communities -- groups of people sharing common emotional norms and expressions . These communities , whether religious groups , families or political factions , use emotions to define their sense of belonging and collective identity , underscoring the role of emotions in shaping social bonds . <p> Gender and emotions : The history of emotions reveals that emotional expression has been gendered throughout history . In many cultures , women were often expected to be more emotionally expressive , nurturing or empathetic , while men were encouraged to be stoic and restrained . Feminist historians have explored how these gendered emotional expectations reinforced social hierarchies and inequalities . <p> The medicalization of emotions : Over time , emotions have increasingly been understood through medical and scientific frameworks . For instance , melancholy , once seen primarily as a spiritual condition , came to be understood as a psychological or medical issue ( now called depression ) . This shift altered both treatments for emotional distress and societal attitudes toward emotional experiences . <p> Major contributors to the history of emotions include : <p> Thomas Dixon , who has explored the shift from the concept of " passions " in early modern thought to the modern idea of " emotions , " highlighting the influence of religious and philosophical ideas on this transformation . <p> Jo Labanyi , whose work focuses on the emotional dimensions of collective memory and trauma in post-Franco Spain , examining how emotions are transmitted and represented in literature and visual culture . <p> William Reddy , who introduced the concept of " emotives , " referring to expressions of emotions that both describe and shape feelings . He has also studied the relationship between emotional expression and political authority , especially during the French Revolution . <p> Barbara Rosenwein , who has demonstrated how different societies create and regulate distinct emotional norms , emphasizing the role of emotional communities in historical contexts . <p> Peter Stearns , who has examined how emotions such as anger , shame and fear have been shaped by changing political , cultural and economic conditions . <p> The history of emotions reveals that emotions are deeply embedded in social structures , power dynamics and cultural contexts . This approach offers a fuller understanding of human history , one that encompasses not only rational decisions and material conditions but also the emotional lives that have influenced -- and been influenced by -- historical change . <p> The history of emotions has reshaped how we understand human experience , revealing that emotions are not merely private , internal states but are deeply intertwined with social , political and cultural contexts . This emerging field shows that emotions are shaped by external forces and play an active role in shaping history itself . <p> Here are some of the key findings from the history of emotions : <p> Emotions are embedded in social structures . Emotions are influenced by the social hierarchies and institutions that structure people 's lives . In any society , there are expectations about how individuals of different classes , genders or statuses should express and experience emotions . For instance , in premodern Europe , noblemen were expected to show controlled restraint , while women , especially of lower status , were often more emotionally expressive in contexts like mourning or religious devotion . These emotional norms reinforced social hierarchies , determining who had the authority to display certain emotions and who was expected to restrain them . <p> Emotions and the rise of modern nation-states . The rise of nation-states brought new emotional expectations , especially through nationalism . Emotions like pride , loyalty and hatred became central to creating national unity , especially in times of war . Totalitarian regimes have often manipulated emotions through propaganda , cultivating fear or devotion to consolidate power and suppress dissent . <p> Emotional regulation tied to power relations . Those in power have historically sought to control and direct emotional expression to maintain authority . Institutions like the church , monarchy and state have dictated the appropriate ways to feel and express emotions , often to maintain social order . The Catholic Church in medieval Europe promoted emotions like guilt , shame and fear to control behavior and ensure adherence to religious norms . In Victorian England , emotional restraint , particularly among middle- and upper-class women , was tied to virtue and decorum . These norms reinforced power structures , keeping certain groups , especially women and the lower class , in subordinate roles . In modern times , governments and corporations use emotional appeals in advertising , propaganda and political messaging to sway public opinion and win elections by appealing not just to policy but to fear , hope and identity . <p> Cultural context shapes emotional experience . Emotions do not exist in isolation ; they are shaped by cultural narratives , practices and values . What is acceptable or encouraged in one culture might be inappropriate or taboo in another . For example , some societies encourage loud , open expressions of grief , while others value more restrained displays of emotion . The language used to describe emotions also reflects cultural context . Ancient Greek had several words for love -- eros ( romantic love ) and agape ( selfless , spiritual love ) -- reflecting different emotional dimensions . Similarly , cultures can have specific emotions that do n't directly translate , such as the German word " schadenfreude , " meaning pleasure in another 's misfortune . <p> Emotions as historical agents . Emotions do not just respond to external events ; they actively shape historical developments . Major social movements -- such as abolition , feminism and civil rights -- are often fueled by emotions like anger , hope and solidarity , driving people to challenge unjust systems . In war , emotions like fear and hatred are cultivated to rally people to a cause . For instance , World War I was sustained in part by national pride and a desire to prove a nation 's greatness , overriding rational concerns about the war 's costs . <p> Conversely , emotions like empathy and compassion have also driven significant historical changes . The abolition of slavery , human rights advancements and humanitarian efforts were often powered by a growing sense of empathy and outrage at injustice . The history of emotions highlights how feelings like guilt , shame or moral indignation can influence laws , policies and cultural transformations . <p> Emotions are integral to lived history , shaping actions , decisions and relationships . By examining emotions , historians gain deeper insight into the motivations behind historical events . Whether exploring the fear that gripped societies during plagues , the religious fervor of the Crusades or the optimism that fueled civil rights movements , the history of emotions offers a fuller understanding of the past . <p> The history of emotions has shown that emotions are deeply embedded in the fabric of historical change . They are both shaped by and help shape social structures , cultural norms and political power . Emotions act as powerful agents in history , influencing events , shaping ideologies and giving rise to cultural and political movements . By studying emotions , we gain a fuller understanding of the complexities of human experience and how emotional life intersects with broader social and historical forces . <p> In a world often consumed by material power -- whether political , military or economic -- the humanities remind us that the most profound and lasting sources of power lie within the human mind . It is through our ideas , values , emotions and perceptions that the true levers of history and progress are moved . <p> The humanities engage deeply with this inner landscape , exploring how ideas shape societies , values define cultures and emotions drive human behavior . They show us that our hopes , fears , ideals and beliefs are not passive reactions but active forces that shape the world around us . <p> Power is not merely wielded through force or wealth , but through the ability to influence hearts and minds -- to inspire , challenge and transform . In an era when technology and economic growth dominate discussions , the humanities offer a vital counterbalance , reminding us that the most transformative changes in society stem from shifts in consciousness . Ideas can liberate or oppress , heal or divide , and through the study of the humanities , we learn to wield this power with responsibility , insight and purpose . <p> Steven Mintz is professor of history at the University of Texas at Austinand the author , most recently , of The Learning-Centered University : Making College a More Developmental , Transformational and Equitable Experience .

@@118966937 <h> Another Voice : Is history on the verge of repeating itself ? <p> Part of a 35-year career for a major New York utility included interest in electricity development history as well as its future . <p> Phil Wilcox is retired from IBEW and lives in Tonawanda . <p> That led to reading an exceptional novel in Lauren Belfer 's " City of Light . " It includes accurate history wrapped in a fictional murder mystery . Among the fascinating parts of the book was the description of the 1901 Pan-American Exposition as a marketing effort by local leadership to showcase our world-leading electric technology . <p> There is also a reference to the assassination of President William McKinley by the anarchist Leon Czolgosz -- an unfortunate blemish for an otherwise spectacular event . The 2021 documentary series , " The Titans That Built America , " described Czolgosz as a hard-working steelworker who was let go after participating in a strike opposing pay cuts . The series went on to describe McKinley as a president bought and paid for by America 's wealthiest people at the time : J.P . Morgan , Andrew Carnegie , John D. Rockefeller and others who wanted less regulation in their quests for more wealth . <p> This frames a frightening similarity to today 's megawealthy who have paid their way into positions of influence for a president-elect who fully embraces pay-to-play policies . The appointments and promises to roll back regulations that protect our food , water and air -- not to mention a complete denial of climate change and any efforts related to necessary emission reductions -- seem to suggest that history is about to repeat itself . <p> The attempt to assassinate a presidential candidate in the recent election cycle saw the perpetrator killed , so it 's at best speculation that he may have had a Czolgosz-type axe to grind . <p> Statistics show the ratio of annual income difference of CEOs and those whose labor provides their wealth has gone from roughly 20-to-1 in the 1960s to nearly 400-to-1 today . <p> If influencers succeed in accumulating more wealth at the expense of societal health , safety and even national security , could there be more frustration targeting select titans ? The decent billionaires in our country , such Bill Gates , understand and support efforts to balance things out . Sadly , they are the rare exceptions , and our country appears to be on a frightening and dangerous trajectory .

But many do n't understand why -- only 58% think that it is caused by humans . And many do n't think that the climate crisis will affect them : only 46% consider themselves personally at risk . <p> These statistics might help to explain why , even though the United States saw record-setting heatwaves , wildfires and mega-storms in 2024 , climate-change discussions remained on the back burner during this year 's presidential election . Campaigners called for cleaner air and water , but few argued for a drastic cut in fossil-fuel use , or discussed how communities can adapt to climate change . President-elect Donald Trump has called climate change a hoax and has promised his campaign backers that he will overturn fossil-fuel regulations . <p> People who do n't think climate change affects them are often apathetic towards , or resistant to , climate action -- despite it being one of the largest long-term threats to everyone 's health and well-being . What is needed to turn things around in the coming years is broad climate literacy . <p> California provides one model . The causes and effects of climate change , as well as mitigation and adaptation methods , are taught in all primary and secondary schools . The state provides some funding to train teachers , but not enough . Ecoliteracy groups , including the non-profit organization Ten Strands and the University of California-based initiative Environmental and Climate Change Literacy Projects , are dedicated to filling the gap . <p> At the university level , climate scientist Veerabhadran Ramanathan and I led a team of researchers who developed educational materials across the University of California system . We developed Bending the Curve -- a library of videos , a textbook , class activities and other teaching resources . Bending the Curve emphasizes equitable solutions in six areas : science , technology , policy and governance , finance , societal behaviour and land-use management . Since its launch in 2017 , thousands of students have used it . <p> The textbook is open access , and the entire library is now being licensed and expanded by organizations such as the American Medical Association and the US National Education Equity Lab , in the United States and beyond . <p> As valuable a tool as Bending the Curve is , it was developed by and for residents of a state that has embraced climate action since the 1970s . Innovative policies such as California 's Global Warming Solutions Act of 2006 , which aims to cut greenhouse-gas emissions to 40% below 1990 levels by 2030 , already receive broad public support . Since September , the San Diego campus of the University of California ( UCSD ) , where I work , has required that all undergraduate students take a course on climate change . <p> But what about states that are not responsive to the urgency of the climate crisis ? In Florida , hit hard by worsening weather extremes , state officials removed mentions of climate change from state laws and some textbooks earlier this year . And , although 90% of the state 's population accept that climate change is happening , only 48% were willing to pay a nominal tax ( of US$10 a month ) to support coastal-resilience efforts . The gap between what people experience , what they think and how they act is striking . <p> It is crucial to move from discussing the climate crisis in terms of collective risks and responsibilities to emphasizing the well-being of individuals , families and local communities . In Florida , a study found that participants were more inclined to change their behaviour -- for example , to invest in local infrastructure and support proactive climate policies -- when they were shown how their neighbourhoods would change if sea levels continued to rise . Even respondents who characterized themselves as " climate deniers " and " conservatives " became concerned when their own futures were at stake . People will enact change only when the challenge becomes personal : not for Mother Earth or for polar bears or , even , for humanity as a whole . <p> Educators can not rely simply on providing scientific knowledge , because research is not what motivates people to change their attitudes and behaviours . Self-interest should figure prominently in climate-education packages . To reach everyone , climate education must be adapted to the location and community , and conveyed in vivid ways . This work should be led by trusted local educators and supported by prominent community members , such as faith leaders , health practitioners and youth mentors ( F. Forman in Health of People , Health of our Planet and our Responsibility 239 -- 250 ; Springer , 2020 ) . <p> At the UCSD Center on Global Justice , which I direct , we have established a cross-border network of four research stations , two in San Diego and two in Tijuana , Mexico , where we work closely with local schools , agencies and faith-based organizations on issues that affect people directly , including heat , poor air quality , flooding and human migration or displacement . We co-lead educational , cultural and environmental activities to increase climate literacy locally . Universities everywhere can develop these kinds of partnership to promote grass-roots education . <p> We are all affected by increasingly intense and frequent weather extremes , unstable food and water systems , the accelerating pace of human displacement , a rapidly unfolding home-insurance disaster and public- and mental-health challenges . This is a collective crisis -- let 's design a climate education that involves everyone , personally .

However , they did agree to expand the UNCCD 's body of independent scientific advisers . September 's Summit of the Future in New York City , organized by UN secretary-general Ant ? nio Guterres also ended with some positive outcomes , including a bold statement that recognizes science as essential to tackling global challenges in its final document , the Pact for the Future . But questions need to be asked as to how this statement can be implemented in the current , highly polarized political climate . <h> Shrinking science <p> It might seem that the world is in a golden age of science in multilateral policymaking . Researchers at universities , in campaign groups and in industry are attending COPs and other meetings in considerable numbers : at least 3,000 scientists attended last year 's COP28 in Dubai , United Arab Emirates ( see ' COP28 in numbers ' ) . They have a variety of roles . Some advise nations ' delegates , the policymakers involved in treaty negotiations . Others are members of official UN science advisory committees . And some come to the meetings to take advantage of the presence of the global media to publicize their research . And yet , despite scientists ' presence , it is evident to observers that COP delegates are not taking research into account in the actual talks . If they were , then negotiating positions would not be as polarized as they are becoming . <p> Source : UN Framework Convention on Climate Change <p> For instance , Nature argued last month that a study of climate finance by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change ( IPCC ) would help to take some of the heat out of disagreements over money . Before the IPCC can commission such a study , a few countries have to propose it . However , until now , there have been no takers . This lack of interest seems like a break from the past , when research helped to shape legally binding agreements , such as the 1989 Montreal Protocol to prohibit the use of ozone-depleting substances , and the 1997 Kyoto Climate Protocol . And in 2015 , research was at the core of the design of the SDGs . <p> Even though groups of scientists in several countries have proposed ways to end plastic pollution , they are struggling to make their voices heard at the talks on a plastics treaty . This is because the UN still has n't organized a formal system for researchers to advise during the discussions . <h> UN under pressure <p> It 's worth reflecting for a moment on why research is currently struggling to have an impact . When the present system of science advice in UN meetings was originally established , the United States and European countries were the world 's largest economies . Their delegates often dominated proceedings , or at least commanded an outsize presence during talks . Much of the research that underpinned UN environmental agreements also came from these nations , as did the scientists observing the talks and many of the world 's influential media outlets covering them . <p> But that world is changing . China is the second largest economy globally and India is on a path to becoming the third . An increasing amount of SDG-related research is now coming from LMICs . At the same time , the place of science in negotiations is affected by this shift in the balance of power . Put simply : when research is performed , or funded , by high-income countries , it is perceived by some in LMICs as being biased in favour of the negotiating positions of the governments of those nations . <p> Overall , the system that scientists use to access and influence UN environmental agreements is under strain . Meeting organizers , delegates and leaders of research institutions must find a way forward together . Science-based decision-making is what will ultimately help the world to resolve the crises it faces . It 's important to understand how and why research is being pushed to the margins and what needs to be done to get policy back on track . 
@@118967532 <p> One of Donald Trump 's closing campaign arguments was that he would deliver a new " golden age " for America . This week , he announced that this Trump-powered golden age has already begun . <p> That 's fitting insofar as Trump has rapidly eclipsed the current president , Joe Biden , in setting expectations and even an agenda for America at home and abroad . It feels as if the clock on the second Trump administration has already started . <p> So has the usual fight over who should get the credit -- or blame -- for the economy the next president inherits . This happens to some extent with every new president , regardless of party and not just on the subject of the economy . <p> As public opinion of Donald Trump , climate change and more show , the press is not as important as journalists and their detractors claim , especially now . <p> Dec. 3 , 2024 <p> Ronald Reagan 's vice president , George H.W. Bush , inherited his economy , but Bush 's aides were quick to note that he also inherited an inevitable recession and a savings and loan crisis from the Gipper . In the closing days of this year 's election , Barack Obama complained that Trump had inherited his economic successes in 2017 . <p> Trump has reason to jump the gun on taking credit for the economy now : It 's doing amazingly well . <p> That 's not to minimize the pain of many Americans or ignore economic problems such as skyrocketing debt , inflation and dislocations in some regions and industries . Even amid a macroeconomic boom , people live in microeconomic circumstances . <p> Advertisement <p> The U.S. economy is nevertheless the envy of the world . Do n't take my word for it : The cover of a special issue of the Economist in October described the American economy as just that , the " Envy of the World , " noting that the United States " has left other rich countries in the dust . " The Financial Times reached the same conclusion this month . <p> The human rights group 's report on the war with Hamas in Gaza acknowledges that prevailing interpretations of international law undermine its accusation . <p> Dec. 10 , 2024 <p> It 's a stark contrast to the 1990s , when many expected Europe 's economies to leave ours in the dust . In 2008 , the European Union 's economy was 10% bigger than that of the United States . By 2022 , it was 23% smaller . The EU grew 21% during this period , but the American economy grew 72% . <p> Today the U.S. economy generates about a quarter of global output . U.S. stocks account for 65% of global equities , while Japan , China and the United Kingdom combined account for just over 10% . If Britain were an American state , it would barely edge out Mississippi -- our poorest state -- in per capita gross domestic product . <p> Advertisement <p> There are many reasons for this . Americans simply workharder than citizens of other rich countries . Our productivity has outstripped the eurozone 's more than 3 to 1 since 2008 . Our business culture is different too : We are the most entrepreneurial country in the world , and we regard business failure not as a cause for shame but as useful experience for the next attempt . America is also better at assimilating immigrants than most countries , and the immigrants we tend to attract generally work very hard . <p> I could go on . The point is that we have had different presidents with very different policies and even more different rhetoric over the last 30 years . But U.S. economic trends -- with the usual dips and spikes -- have been largely positive through all of those presidencies . <p> As the Manhattan Institute 's Brian Riedl put it in National Affairs , " The notion that there is a simple partisan pattern to the health of the economy is an extension of the exaggerated politicization of our understanding of contemporary American life . " <p> Recent dissatisfaction with the economy , spurred by inflation , fueled the idea that America was doing especially awful under Biden . Again , we live in microeconomies , so it 's understandable that many people had that view . But we 've still been doing better than pretty much everyone else . <p> Trump 's focus on the economic downside was typical for a presidential challenger and fair enough . But he was wrong to suggest that our competitors were eating our lunch . <p> None of this is to suggest that presidents and their economic policies do n't matter . It 's just that they do n't matter as much as presidents and their partisans claim they do . <p> Jonah Goldberg is editor in chief of the Dispatch and has been a Los Angeles Times Opinion columnist since 2005 . He holds the Asness Chair in Applied Liberty at the American Enterprise Institute . He was previously senior editor at National Review and lives in Washington , D.C.

When you tell kids a real king lives here , their ears will perk up ! <p> What to do ? Start monitoring flights months in advance and consider European airlines . ( Low-cost carrier Norwegian Air often has round-trip , nonstop London flights from several major U.S. cities for less than $500 . ) On your first full morning in London , check out the Changing of the Guard where the soldiers march out in their trademark red coats and fuzzy black hats . It starts at 11 a.m. ( 10 a.m. on Sundays ) but get there at least a half-hour early so the little ones can see . If the royal flag is flying , the King is in residence . St. James Park is a stone 's throw away and has a lovely playground . <p> " If you 're a baseball family , the Baseball Hall of Fame in Cooperstown is a ca n't miss destination . The Hall of Fame is interactive , informative , and perfect for the young all-star in your family to dream big about making their mark in the MLB . As the little sister in the family I got dragged to too many baseball games to count , but this museum remains one of my favorite family trips to date . " -- Kate McCarthy , the senior social media editor at Shop TODAY <p> Where to stay : Stay on the water at Lake ' N Pines Motel where guests have an outdoor pool , an indoor pool and a video arcade room . Downtown , The Railroad Inn has lofts that comfortably sleep families of six . <p> Where to stay : With a No. 2 ranking on TripAdvisor , The River Inn near Foggy Bottom metro station is a great affordable option . Closer to the National Mall , you a comfortable room at Sofitel Washington , D.C. <p> " As a Massachusetts native , Plimoth Plantation was a hot field trip destination during my school years , and for good reason . The outdoor recreation of a 17th-century village makes kids ( and adults ) feel like they 're stepping back into time . The best part is that there are actors who fully stay in character like it 's the year 1627 , so while there are plenty of moments to learn about what life was like then , kids will also get a kick out of asking them questions about modern life and seeing the confusion on the actor 's faces . " -- Kate McCarthy , the senior social media editor at Shop TODAY <p> Best for ages : 8-12 <p> Why go ? It 's like stepping back in time to the 17th century , when the pilgrims arrived here from England . <p> What to do : Get a look at Plymouth Rock , where colonists first set foot on American soil . You wo n't believe how tiny it is . Costumed actors recreate what it was like on the crossing and in the settlement . Learn about Native American cooking , crafts and culture at the Wampanoag Homesite . Visit the nearby Plimoth Grist Mill where you can see how they grind corn and even buy it to take home !

To submit a letter to the editor for publication , write to letters@nytimes.com. <h> 2024 The Year in Pictures <h> Far From Ordinary <p> By Carolyn Ryan <p> When shots were fired at a campaign rally for former President Donald J. Trump on a July evening in Butler , Pa. , the veteran New York Times photographer Doug Mills was just a few feet from him . As the Secret Service rushed toward Mr. Trump , Mr. Mills 's heart pounded when he realized what was happening . <p> Then instinct took over . Mr. Mills kept taking pictures , at an extremely fast shutter speed of one eight-thousandth of a second , capturing an image that illustrates the magnitude of that moment : Mr. Trump , his face streaked with blood , his fist raised in defiance . <p> This year was made up of such extraordinary moments . And Times photographers captured them in extraordinary images . The Year in Pictures brings you the most powerful , evocative and history-making of those images -- and allows you to see the biggest stories of 2024 through our photographers ' eyes . <p> The presidential campaign -- full of twists and turns -- provided some of our most memorable photos . Kenny Holston captured a shaky President Biden struggling to find his footing in what turned out to be his only debate of the 2024 election . Erin Schaff conveyed the exhilaration surrounding Vice President Kamala Harris in the short sprint of her campaign . And Todd Heisler brought home the excitement of an 8-year-old girl in pigtails , Ms. Harris 's great-niece , who watched with pride as Ms. Harris accepted her party 's nomination for president . <p> Yet even as the American political campaign intensified , wars ground on overseas , creating new dangers and obstacles for our photojournalists determined to document the fighting . The war between Hamas and Israel escalated into a regional conflict , and our photographers depicted the Israeli airstrikes on Lebanon , the families forced to flee their homes and the neighborhoods reduced to rubble . <p> When Israeli forces recovered the bodies of six hostages in Gaza , our photographers revealed the pain of the captives ' families as they cried out at their loved ones ' funerals after 11 months of anguished waiting . And last month , Samar Abu Elouf , a Palestinian photographer for The Times , delivered some of the most indelible images of the year : a series of portraits of Gazans horribly injured in the war , including children who had lost arms , legs or eyes . <p> Children were also central to the work of Lynsey Addario , a veteran photographer who has been chronicling the war in Ukraine since Russia first invaded in 2022 . Ms. Addario 's images tell the stories of young Ukrainians with cancer whose treatment was disrupted by the war , often with devastating results . One , a 5-year-old girl whose chemotherapy was upended by the Russian invasion , ultimately lost her life . <p> Our photographers embrace their calling of bearing witness to history , showing readers the atrocities and the suffering that might otherwise be overlooked . But they also see their mission more broadly , and aim to depict the richness and color of life by regularly bringing us pictures that delight and surprise . <p> Take the photo by Hiroko Masuike from the ticker-tape parade in October for the New York Liberty women 's basketball team . The young fans pictured radiate a kind of awe-struck joy , screaming to the players by name . Or the photographs that show the sense of wonder on the faces of people at Niagara Falls as they bask in the magic of a solar eclipse in April . <p> We hope you can spend some time with these pictures , and take in our photographers ' reflections on them . This collection of images is a way to remember the year , but it is also , we hope , an opportunity to better understand their craft and their devotion to producing the world 's best photojournalism . <h> January <p> Arivaca , Ariz. , Jan. 13 Migrants climbing over the border wall between Mexico and a ranch in Arizona .
